site_narrative.tagline: 20+ years of software engineering experience. Over the last 10-11 years specifically, I've worked on high-throughput, latency-sensitive distributed systems at different scales and constraints - from microsecond-level C++ engineering, to reliable distributed event handling, to a banking ledger built from scratch that has to be fast and provably correct. I've done this hands-on across India, France, and Singapore, working directly with different teams, customers, and stakeholders in each - which has shaped an ability to adapt quickly to different team cultures and ways of working.

pillars.title: High-Throughput, Latency-Critical Backend Systems
pillars.text: I've worked at multiple points on the throughput/latency spectrum - from a microsecond-level C++ component under a ~2ms budget, to distributed event handlers processing hundreds of thousands and then millions of messages a day, to a banking ledger processing hundreds of thousands of transactions daily. Each of these had a different bottleneck, and each needed a different engineering approach.

pillars.title: Distributed Backend Systems Reliability
pillars.text: A recurring focus across my recent roles has been finding and eliminating systemic reliability gaps in event-driven, multi-service systems - particularly around asynchronous, vendor-originated events that don't fit neatly into existing retry or correlation patterns. I've done this for hotel-booking traffic and for banking core-systems alike.

pillars.title: Backend Platform & Product Architecture
pillars.text: I architect end-to-end platforms for new products - travel/hospitality and financial alike - from initial design through full-scale migration, and drive cross-team engineering standards beyond my own team's boundaries.

case_studies.title: Building a Core Banking Ledger From Scratch
case_studies.problem: GXS Bank's lending business needed a resilient, high-throughput ledger core. Extending the bank's existing vendor core banking platform - licensed primarily for deposit accounts - to also cover lending was cost-prohibitive for what the lending platform actually needed, making an in-house ledger the more viable path.
case_studies.approach: I designed and built FinSync from scratch: a ledger platform that cleanly separates core ledger state (accounts, balance partitions, atomic posting-instruction batches) from product-specific business rules, which live in a companion policy service. The system is fully event-driven, using Kafka for account initialization and posting approvals, and relies on a set of data-integrity patterns I designed specifically for this scale: a serialized single-writer update pattern to eliminate lock contention, atomic multi-statement transactions, an outbox/relay pattern for reliable event publication, and partitioning message queues by loan product type to scale ingestion horizontally, backed by a resilience layer of context-aware blocking retries with dead-letter-queue fallback.
case_studies.outcome: As of Q3 2026, FinSync powers the entire rebuilt lending platform, processing ~800K transactions/day, projected to reach ~2M/day by Q4 2026, after a full migration of every partner off the legacy system.

case_studies.title: Scaling a Bank's Deposit Platform: Rebuilding Account Lifecycle Workflows
case_studies.problem: GXS Bank's deposit product line was set to scale beyond its core savings-account product into pockets and time-deposit products, but the account lifecycle underneath it couldn't scale with it. Account creation on the deposits core microservice was built as a synchronous call, even though the underlying core banking platform's account and plan entities were asynchronous - a mismatch that was already generating incidents and would only get worse as more products launched on top of it. Account closures had the same problem from a different angle: the core banking platform emitted multiple asynchronous closure events for the same request without consistent context to correlate them, and closures would intermittently fail during end-of-day batch processing due to stale interest-accrual balances. Neither gap could be safely scaled past without first being fixed.
case_studies.approach: I rebuilt both halves of the account lifecycle so the platform could scale to new products without carrying its incident rate with it. For account creation, I helped the team introduce a process-orchestration tool, already proven at sister digital banks, to bridge the sync/async gap - then went further: the existing internal retry library only worked with internal DTOs, so I designed and built a retry engine library that works with third-party vendor DTOs from the core banking platform, with configurable retries. For closures, I redesigned the workflow around Kafka and SQS to reliably correlate and retry the same closure request across multiple uncorrelated vendor events, and added a delayed-closure mechanism that parks closure requests on a queue during the end-of-day processing window to avoid transient balance-timing failures.
case_studies.outcome: Both initiatives were first-of-their-kind across all three sister digital banks at the time. Together, they took the deposits account lifecycle from a synchronous, incident-prone bottleneck to a foundation that scales cleanly across product types - production incidents from account creation and closures came down close to zero, and the platform could take on new deposit products with confidence.

case_studies.title: Three Stages of Growth at Amadeus (2015-2022)
case_studies.problem: Across three roles at a previous company, Amadeus, on its core hotel IT platform, I took on progressively larger classes of problems: first a microsecond-level latency constraint, then distributed reliability at scale, then cross-platform integration at even greater scale.
case_studies.approach: Starting in Nice, France (2015-2018), I helped build a booking component in C++ under a ~2ms end-to-end budget, where individual operations had to run in microseconds - a problem of raw execution speed on a small, contained component. Moving to Bengaluru (2018-2021), I led a gateway event handler processing several hundred thousand messages/day over internal queues (C++/Python), where the problem shifted to reliability - designing retry and error-handling for a distributed system rather than optimizing one component. As Principal Engineer (2021-2022), the same class of problem returned at millions of messages/day, now spanning vendor systems and real-time booking traffic - I redesigned the messaging core around Kafka and extended it into Java alongside C++.
case_studies.outcome: Each stage was a different kind of engineering problem, not just a bigger version of the last: machine-level performance, then distributed-systems reliability, then cross-platform integration at scale - the same progression of thinking I later applied to banking core-systems.
